description: Who Homer was, oral epic poetry, and the Odyssey's place at the start of Greek literature.
content_html:
Who Was Homer?

The Odyssey is one of the oldest surviving works of Western literature, and tradition attributes it to a poet called Homer. Ancient writers generally believed Homer was a blind bard from Ionia — the western coast of what is now Turkey — who composed both the Iliad and the Odyssey. Modern scholars, however, debate whether a single poet called Homer ever existed, whether the two epics were composed by the same person, and whether the poems we have today were the work of one genius or the result of centuries of collaborative oral tradition. What matters for the exam is understanding the nature of the tradition that produced these poems.

The ancient Greeks themselves held Homer in extraordinary esteem. They called him simply “the Poet,” as though no other poet needed naming. His works were the foundation of Greek education: schoolchildren learnt passages by heart, rhapsodes (professional reciters) performed them at festivals, and philosophers quoted them to settle arguments about ethics and the gods.

Key Fact

The Odyssey was composed and performed in an oral tradition. The performer — a bard or rhapsode — used a stock repertoire of formulae, repeated phrases and set-piece scenes to compose the poem in performance, rather than reading from a written text.

What Makes the Odyssey an Epic?

An epic poem is a long narrative poem that deals with heroes and their deeds on a grand scale. The Odyssey has several defining features that mark it out as epic. It is composed in dactylic hexameter, the traditional metre of Greek epic — a rolling, stately rhythm that feels weightier than ordinary speech. It opens with an invocation of the Muse, asking the goddess of poetry to inspire the telling: the poem begins by asking the Muse to tell of “the man of many ways” — Odysseus. This signals immediately that the story is not merely entertainment but a divinely inspired account of great deeds.

Another epic convention is beginning in medias res — that is, starting the story in the middle of the action rather than at the beginning. When the Odyssey opens, Odysseus has already been wandering for ten years. We learn the earlier stages of his journey through his own narration to the Phaeacians in Books 9 and 10. This technique creates dramatic suspense and allows Homer to concentrate on the most significant episodes.

Three key oral-formulaic techniques appear throughout the Odyssey. First, epithets are fixed labels attached to characters: Odysseus is repeatedly called “resourceful Odysseus,” “godlike Odysseus,” or “the great tactician.” The rosy-fingered Dawn appears at the start of many mornings. These tags are not decorative accidents — they serve a practical function, allowing the performer to fill a particular part of the line while also reinforcing a character’s defining quality.

Second, formulae are repeated phrases used to describe recurring actions — drinking, eating, praying, greeting a guest. When Odysseus arrives at a new palace, Homer uses a set sequence of reception scenes that mirrors the rules of xenia. Third, Homeric similes — also called extended similes — pause the action to compare events to scenes from everyday life. When Odysseus finally kills the leading suitor, Homer compares the fallen man to an acrobat tumbling off a stool. These similes are vivid, surprising and ground the heroic world in the real world of the audience.

The Structure of the Odyssey

The Odyssey is divided into 24 books. The first four books follow Odysseus’s son Telemachus as he searches for news of his father — a section often called the Telemachy. Books 5–8 introduce Odysseus, stranded on the island of Calypso and eventually reaching the Phaeacians. Books 9–12 are Odysseus’s own first-person account of his adventures — a story within the story. Books 13–24 describe his return to Ithaca, his disguise as a beggar, the recognition scenes and the final bloody revenge on the suitors.

This structure is highly crafted. By placing Books 9–12 as a first-person flashback told by Odysseus to the Phaeacians, Homer allows the hero to be his own storyteller — which itself reveals something important about his character. Odysseus is a man of words as much as of deeds, and his ability to tell a compelling story is part of what makes him a great hero.

Key Fact

The Odyssey consists of 24 books. The prescribed books for study are Books 9, 10, 19, 21 and 22. Book 9 contains the Cyclops episode; Book 10 the encounter with Circe; Book 19 the recognition of Odysseus by his nurse Eurycleia; Book 21 the contest of the bow; and Book 22 the slaughter of the suitors.

A common misconception is that oral poetry must be imprecise or low quality. In fact, the scholarship of Milman Parry and Albert Lord in the 20th century showed that oral poets in the Balkans could compose thousands of lines of technically accomplished verse in performance. The repetitions, formulae and epithets in Homer are not signs of laziness — they are the tools of a sophisticated oral craft. The question of when the poems were written down is separate from the question of when they were first composed: the standard scholarly view is that the poems reached roughly their current form around the 8th century BC, and were written down during the 6th or 7th century BC.

It is also a misconception to think of Homer’s poems as simple myths invented for entertainment. The Greeks regarded them as a record of a real heroic age, a time when great men interacted directly with the gods. Modern archaeology has confirmed that a wealthy Bronze Age civilisation — the Mycenaean world — did exist, though the poems blend historical memory with legend and imagination in ways we cannot fully separate.

Themes and the Odyssey’s Appeal

The Odyssey is built around a series of powerful, interlocking themes. Nostos — the desire to return home — drives every choice Odysseus makes. The poem asks: what is it that makes a place “home”? Is it a physical location, a wife and son, a kingdom, or an identity? Every obstacle Odysseus faces tests whether his longing for Ithaca is stronger than the temptations placed in his way.

The tension between civilised and barbaric behaviour runs through the poem. Every new land Odysseus visits is measured against Greek standards of civilised life: do they practise xenia? Do they have proper laws and agriculture? The Cyclops Polyphemus fails every test. Circe begins as a monster but comes to embody a kind of civilised hospitality. These contrasts are not just entertaining — they define the civilised world that Odysseus is fighting to return to.
exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to ‘describe’ a feature of the Odyssey such as an epithet or a simile, give a specific example and explain what effect it creates — do not just define the term. The single biggest examiner concern is over-narration: students retelling what happens rather than analysing what Homer is doing and why. For an ‘explain’ question about oral composition, name the technique (epithet, formula, in medias res), give the specific example from the text, and say what purpose it serves for performer or audience. For essay questions, use named sources: quote the opening invocation, cite the specific books, and name the technical terms.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Odyssey is an oral epic attributed to Homer — composed in the oral tradition using epithets, formulae and extended similes, and structured to begin in medias res.
  • Epic conventions include the invocation of the Muse, dactylic hexameter, heroic subject matter and formal narrative scale; the five prescribed books (9, 10, 19, 21, 22) cover the adventures, the recognition and the revenge.
  • Central themes are nostos (the drive to return home), xenia (hospitality), and the contrast between civilised and barbaric behaviour — all of which are tested through Odysseus’s encounters on his journey.

practice_questions.text: Name the Greek term for the longing to return home that drives Odysseus throughout the poem.
Describe what is meant by an epithet in Homeric epic poetry, giving one example from the Odyssey.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: a repeated descriptive phrase or fixed label attached to a character (or similar). 1 mark for a correct example, e.g. 'resourceful Odysseus' / 'godlike Odysseus' / 'rosy-fingered Dawn'. 1 mark for explaining its function: fills a metrical slot in the line / reinforces the character's defining quality / aids performance.

practice_questions.text:
Read this paraphrase of the opening of the Odyssey:

'The poet asks his Muse to sing of the resourceful man who wandered many years after the fall of Troy, suffering greatly on sea and suffering greatly on land, as he struggled to save his own life and the lives of his companions. Yet for all his striving, he could not save them — they were destroyed by their own recklessness.'

What does this opening passage suggest about the way Homer presents Odysseus and his companions? Refer to specific details from the passage in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses at least two specific details from the passage with developed explanation of what they reveal about character or theme. Likely points: 'resourceful man' — the epithet immediately defines Odysseus by his intelligence and adaptability rather than strength; the contrast between Odysseus's survival and the crew's destruction establishes the theme of self-reliance; 'their own recklessness' — suggests the crew bear responsibility for their fate and signals the poem's interest in the theme of justice; the invocation of the Muse establishes epic authority and signals divine inspiration. Candidates who refer to specific words or phrases score more highly.
Secure: Two details identified and explained, without full analytical development.
Developing: One detail identified and explained.
Emerging: General comment on the passage with little specific reference.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the structure of the Odyssey — beginning in medias res — is effective for the audience.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying in medias res correctly (the story starts in the middle of the action, with Odysseus already at sea for ten years). 1 mark for an effect on the audience (creates immediate drama / suspense / raises questions about the backstory). 1 mark for development (the earlier adventures are then told by Odysseus himself in Books 9–10, making him his own storyteller). 1 mark for linking to characterisation (this technique itself reveals Odysseus's skill with words and self-presentation).

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that the oral tradition is the most important feature for understanding Homer's Odyssey? Refer to a range of named sources and give a supported judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained argument that engages with both sides. For: oral composition explains epithets (e.g. 'resourceful Odysseus'), formulae (reception scenes, set-piece descriptions), extended similes and structural repetition; understanding the tradition helps us interpret the text as a performance rather than a fixed literary work; the invocation of the Muse signals the poem's oral origins. Against: the poem's thematic richness — nostos, xenia, justice, civilisation vs barbarism — is independent of its oral origins; the sophisticated in medias res structure and the nested narrative of Books 9–12 show literary artistry; the prescribed books reward close reading regardless of oral context. Top answers will name specific episodes and technical features, and reach a clear, supported judgement.
Secure: Two points on each side with at least one named source.
Developing: Mostly one-sided with limited source use.
Emerging: General discussion, few named sources, no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Homer uses language techniques to tell the story of the Odyssey effectively.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two techniques (e.g. epithets and extended similes, or formulae and in medias res), each with a specific example and developed explanation of effect. For epithets: fixed labels like 'resourceful Odysseus' signal character instantly and aid oral performance; for extended similes: comparing Odysseus attacking the suitors to a natural phenomenon grounds the heroic action in vivid, relatable imagery and slows the pace for dramatic effect.
Secure: Two techniques each with an example and a clear explanation.
Developing: Two techniques named but explanation limited; or one technique fully explained.
Emerging: General reference to 'language' without naming or explaining specific techniques.

glossary_terms.definition: The ancient Greek poet to whom the Iliad and the Odyssey are traditionally attributed; his identity as a single historical person remains debated.
A tradition in which poetry is composed and transmitted through spoken performance rather than writing, relying on stock phrases, standard scenes and the performer's memory.
A Greek professional singer who performed epic poetry from memory at festivals and public gatherings.
A long narrative poem on a grand scale, dealing with heroes, gods and momentous events, composed in formal verse and following traditional conventions.
A formal appeal to a divine being at the start of a poem, asking for inspiration and assistance in telling the story.
Latin for 'in the middle of things'; a narrative technique where the story begins at a late point in the action, with earlier events revealed through flashback.
A repeated descriptive phrase attached to a character or object in epic poetry, which fills a certain metrical slot in the line and acts as a shorthand identity tag.
An extended comparison in epic poetry that develops over several lines, comparing something in the main narrative to something from everyday life.
The craft of composing and delivering poetry in the oral tradition, using standard phrases, scenes and structural patterns to aid composition and memory.
The Greek concept of the longing or drive to return home, a central motivation for Odysseus throughout the poem.
The Greek code of hospitality, which required hosts to welcome strangers with food and shelter before asking their name or business, and guests to behave respectfully in return.
